programmeDeliveryTrackRecord:
Wootlab Foundation has a strong track record of designing and implementing large-scale digital skills, entrepreneurship, education, and capacity-building programmes across Nigeria and beyond. Its delivery experience spans partnerships with government institutions, Microsoft, multinational organisations, financial institutions, development partners, and private-sector organisations, with programmes reaching beneficiaries across multiple states and underserved communities.

Key delivery experience includes:
Large-scale digital skills delivery: Over 120,000 Nigerian youths trained through the Federal Government–Microsoft Digital Skills Nigeria initiative, alongside programmes reaching tens of thousands of additional beneficiaries across states.
Digital community implementation: Operationalisation of 50 Digital Community Centres across 17 states, managing 100 facilitators and training over 21,393 beneficiaries between August and May.

Youth and employability programmes: More than 26,000 beneficiaries trained in Anambra across digital skills, entrepreneurship and career pathways, with selected beneficiaries receiving laptops and internship opportunities.

Public-sector capacity building: Delivery of digital upskilling programmes for civil servants, including 210 OHCSF participants in 2024 and 500 civil servants in 2025 across key federal institutions.

Teacher development: Implementation of the Seplat Teachers Empowerment Programme, including 650 teachers trained in 2025 and a cumulative 1,984 teachers empowered since inception.

Women and girls in technology: Programmes including RevUp Women and Girls in ICT initiatives, reaching women entrepreneurs and over 335 female secondary-school students, respectively.

Digital learning infrastructure: Extensive deployment of the Microsoft Community Training (MCT) Platform, with over 300,000 registered learners through 57 partner organisations and programmes since 2022.
Enterprise development: Delivery of entrepreneurship programmes, including support to 375 business owners in Kwara, with 170 businesses qualifying for loan support and over ₦102 million disbursed to eligible businesses.
Inclusive digital skills: Training of over 10,800 young people across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe, with deliberate inclusion of women and Persons with Disabilities.

Overall, this track record demonstrates Wootlab Foundation’s capacity to manage multi-stakeholder programmes, deliver at scale, leverage digital learning platforms, coordinate distributed implementation teams, and translate training investments into measurable participation, certification, employability and enterprise outcomes.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity:
Gender Equality, Social Inclusion and Equity (GESI) will be integrated throughout the programme lifecycle, from mobilisation and beneficiary selection to training, assessment, employment and ongoing monitoring. The programme will maintain a 50/50 gender balance and target at least 5% participation from young people who are Not in Employment, Education or Training (NEET), while deliberately creating opportunities for Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) and other marginalised and underserved groups.

To promote gender parity, participation will be actively monitored from the application stage through enrolment, attendance, completion, certification and placement, with all relevant data disaggregated by gender. Targeted mobilisation strategies will be used to increase female participation, including engagement with women’s groups, faith-based organisations, female ambassadors, recruiters and trainers. Female application and conversion rates will also be monitored by state and mobilisation channel to identify and address gaps in participation.

The programme will also prioritise operational accessibility and safe participation for all beneficiaries. Training venues will be selected to promote safety and accessibility, while flexible schedules will be considered to accommodate participants with different needs. Where approved and feasible, additional support such as childcare or transport assistance may be provided to reduce barriers to participation. Attendance, retention and withdrawal patterns will be monitored to identify challenges that may disproportionately affect vulnerable participants.

For Persons with Disabilities, the programme will actively create pathways for participation through targeted mobilisation and partnerships with organisations such as the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD), the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities (JONAPWD) and other disability-focused organisations. Accessibility assessments will inform programme delivery, while participation, reasonable accommodation, completion and placement outcomes for PWDs will be specifically tracked.

The programme will further adopt targeted approaches to reach NEETs and other vulnerable groups, including young people in underserved communities and internally displaced persons (IDPs). Community-based partners, social-welfare actors and other relevant stakeholders will support outreach to these groups. Where required, participants will receive reasonable accommodation, including assistive technologies, adapted learning materials and individual support plans, based on identified needs.

GESI considerations will extend beyond training into employment and placement. The programme will engage employers that demonstrate disability-inclusive practices and provide workplace-readiness and placement support to participants. Employer inclusion practices and PWD placement outcomes will be monitored to ensure that inclusion is reflected not only in programme participation but also in access to employment opportunities.

Overall accountability for GESI implementation will be supported through GESI Specialist oversight, weekly monitoring and quarterly inclusion reporting. Participation and outcome data will be reviewed regularly to identify disparities, track progress against inclusion targets and implement corrective actions where necessary. This approach will ensure that GESI is treated as a core programme delivery principle rather than a standalone activity.

Wootlab will engage designated institutional staff and faculty as key implementation partners throughout the programme. During mobilisation, we will work with relevant focal persons to communicate programme objectives, identify eligible beneficiaries and facilitate access to existing student, alumni and entrepreneurship networks.

We will establish clear institutional focal points who will coordinate with the Wootlab implementation team and support communication between the programme and relevant university structures. Staff and faculty will also be oriented on the programme's objectives, eligibility requirements, referral process and available enterprise support so they can effectively identify and recommend suitable beneficiaries.

beneficiaryReferralPlan:
Beneficiaries will be identified through a combination of institution-led mobilisation, targeted outreach and structured application and screening processes. Wootlab will work with institutional focal persons, entrepreneurship centres, career services, faculties, student affairs units and alumni networks to reach eligible students, graduates and entrepreneurs.

Institutions will be provided with clear eligibility and referral criteria to enable staff and faculty to identify potential beneficiaries, particularly individuals with viable business ideas, existing enterprises or clear entrepreneurial potential who can benefit from the programme's support.

Wootlab will complement institutional referrals with direct mobilisation through its established digital and community networks, ensuring that outreach extends beyond beneficiaries already connected to entrepreneurship centres. All applicants will undergo a transparent screening process against agreed programme criteria, with attention to inclusion and equitable participation.

Beneficiary data will be captured through a structured registration and verification process, allowing Wootlab to track participation, support provided, enterprise progress and outcomes throughout the programme. This approach will combine the reach and institutional knowledge of partner institutions with Wootlab's experience in large-scale beneficiary mobilisation and programme delivery.
monitoringReportingSystems:
Wootlab Foundation uses structured digital systems for beneficiary registration, attendance, participation, performance tracking and post-programme monitoring. Our programme delivery is supported by digital dashboards and data collection tools that enable real-time tracking of beneficiary engagement and programme outputs across multiple locations.

We use standardised data collection and verification processes to ensure that beneficiary information is captured accurately and can be disaggregated by relevant indicators such as gender, location, institution and programme participation. Programme teams regularly review data to identify gaps, monitor performance against targets and inform implementation decisions.

We provide periodic implementation and outcome reports to partners and stakeholders, supported by beneficiary-level data, attendance records, activity reports and documented results.

For iDICE, we will maintain a centralised monitoring framework covering beneficiary onboarding, enterprise support activities, mentorship, milestones, referrals and post-programme outcomes, with clear reporting responsibilities and data protection protocols.
sustainabilityPlan:
Wootlab Foundation's sustainability approach combines strategic partnerships, programme diversification and the ability to mobilise resources from development partners, private-sector organisations and institutional funders. We do not intend for enterprise support activities to depend solely on a single funding source.

Wootlab will leverage its established relationships with development organisations, government institutions, technology partners, universities and private-sector stakeholders to identify opportunities for continued enterprise development support. We will also pursue competitive grants, corporate social responsibility partnerships and co-funded programmes aligned with youth employment, entrepreneurship, digital skills and inclusive economic development.

In addition, Wootlab's wider organisational ecosystem, including its technical and talent development capabilities, provides opportunities to connect trained entrepreneurs and skilled beneficiaries to private-sector opportunities. Lessons, tools and institutional relationships developed through the programme will be integrated into future enterprise and employability initiatives, creating a foundation for continued support beyond the iDICE programme.

Our sustainability model therefore focuses on diversifying funding, strengthening partnerships and building institutional capacity, rather than relying on one programme or revenue stream.
employmentPathway:
Wootlab will design the programme around a clear progression from enterprise support to income generation, employment and business growth. Beneficiaries will first be assessed to understand their skills, business stage and career or enterprise goals. Based on this assessment, they will receive targeted capacity development, mentorship and practical support relevant to their pathway.

For employment-oriented beneficiaries, Wootlab will facilitate exposure to industry, career guidance, skills development and referrals to relevant employment opportunities. Beneficiaries demonstrating the required competencies will be connected to employers and talent networks, while those pursuing entrepreneurship will receive enterprise-focused mentoring and support to strengthen their business models, customer acquisition and readiness for growth.

Wootlab will track key transition points, including completion, employment or self-employment, enterprise activity, referrals and income-generating outcomes. This creates a practical pathway of identification → assessment → skills/enterprise support → industry exposure → referral → employment or enterprise growth → post-programme tracking.

Our experience in digital skills, employability and talent development, alongside the capabilities of Wootlab Innovations, will enable us to strengthen the transition between programme participation and real economic opportunities.

institutionalCoordinationPlan:
The work  that we do at Mentor-Box is deeply anchored in existing public sector frameworks, most notably through our foundational partnership with the Kogi State Enterprise Development Agency (KEDA). Because of our historical executive and board-level involvement with the agency, we don't just work alongside the government, we help bridge the gap between state economic policy and the grassroots entrepreneurs who need it most. This ensures our programs align seamlessly with official development goals and give our trainees direct pathways to state-backed support and funding.

Beyond that, we are actively building the Kogi Young Innovators Community, creating a dedicated pipeline that catches students while they are still in school and transitions them into tech-enabled entrepreneurship and innovation before graduation.

We have built a genuine, working relationship with the Student Union Government at the Federal University Lokoja. By actively co-implementing projects with the student leadership body particularly during student union weeks, we get authentic buy in, high engagement, and direct access to young people who are ready to build, learn, and lead.

Alumni & Leadership Networks We know that a training program is only as good as what happens after it ends. This network plugs our graduates straight into an elite, active ecosystem of changemakers and entrepreneurs, giving them lifelong peer support, mentorship, and collaboration opportunities long after their time with Mentor-Box is done.
staffFacultyEngagementPlan:
To ensure programme success and sustainability, engaging institutional staff and faculty is critical to embedding our work into the very fabric of the academic environment  rather than treating it as an outside intervention. 

 Co-Design and Curriculum Integration We don't approach faculty with a rigid, ready-made package. Instead, we engage department heads, entrepreneurship center directors, and lecturers in collaborative co-design sessions. By aligning our digital skills, financial literacy, and business development modules with their existing departmental frameworks and institutional goals, we position our programs as an enhancement rather than a disruption to their academic calendar. This collaborative curriculum design ensures that faculty members view the initiative as their own.

Capacity Building and Train-the-Trainer Models To foster long-term institutional ownership, we deploy a Train-the-Trainer approach. Rather than relying solely on external facilitators from Mentor-Box, we actively involve internal staff and faculty in our training workshops, bootcamps, and accelerator programs. We equip them with modern pedagogical tools, AI-enabled administrative workflows, and practical tech frameworks. By upskilling the faculty first, we turn them into active champions who can independently mentor students, sustain the modules long after initial project cycles, and drive institutional capacity from within.

Incentivized Collaboration and Recognition We recognize that faculty members juggle heavy teaching, research, and administrative loads. Our engagement plan incorporates structured incentives, including formal co-facilitation credits, collaborative research opportunities stemming from our project data, and joint recognition during milestone events like demo days and graduation ceremonies. By highlighting their leadership in reports, policy roundtables, and ecosystem showcases, we elevate their profiles within the broader academic and innovation landscape.
beneficiaryReferralPlan:
To ensure our programs reach the right people especially women and NEET youth who might otherwise slip through the cracks our beneficiary identification and referral process relies on a mix of grassroots community mobilization, institutional partnerships, and practical, aptitude-based screening.

Grassroots and Community-Level Mobilization

We don’t rely solely on online flyers or passive digital ads to find participants. Instead, we use our deep roots in the Kogi Startup Community and local grassroots networks to meet people where they are. We partner directly with community leaders, youth groups, and local stakeholders to run town-hall sensitizations and awareness drives. This boots-on-the-ground approach ensures that marginalized groups, informal entrepreneurs, and young people in off-grid or semi-urban areas are actively sought out and informed about the opportunity.

Institutional and Campus-Based Referrals

To capture students and young innovators within formal structures, we tap directly into our network of academic and enterprise partners. We work closely with campus bodies like the Student Union Government at Federal University Lokoja, entrepreneurship centers like the EDC at Kogi State Polytechnic, and faculty departments. These institutional allies act as trusted referral channels, directing ambitious students, recent graduates, and campus-based founders straight into our mobilization funnel.

Agency and Government-Backed Channels

Through our strategic partnerships with public sector bodies like the Kogi State Enterprise Development Agency (KEDA) and state ICT frameworks, we leverage existing databases of micro-entrepreneurs and civic applicants. For initiatives focused on business development or grant readiness (such as past integrations with NG-CARES), KEDA and aligned agencies help channel validated entrepreneurs who already meet specific enterprise criteria directly into our cohorts.

Aptitude-Based and Inclusion-Focused Screening

Traditional application processes often shut out the exact demographics we aim to elevate—such as NEET youth who lack formal CVs or women stepping back from the workforce. We replace rigid academic screening with alternative, capability-based assessment models. Our screening looks at raw problem-solving aptitude, baseline digital curiosity, and community endorsements. For female-targeted programs, our outreach explicitly addresses and accommodates the realities of primary caregivers, ensuring the application and onboarding process is accessible, welcoming, and barrier-free.
monitoringReportingSystems:

sustainabilityPlan:

governanceStructure:
OPOLO Global Innovation Ltd. maintains a clear governance and leadership structure designed to ensure strategic oversight, accountability, effective programme delivery, financial integrity and measurable impact in the execution of its Enterprise Support Organisation (ESO) mandate.

Governance Structure

The Board of Directors provides the highest level of governance and strategic oversight. The Board is responsible for approving strategic direction, providing oversight of organisational performance, financial management, risk, compliance and major institutional commitments.

Board oversight is supported by key governance responsibilities covering:

Finance, Audit & Risk – financial accountability, internal controls, procurement, audit and risk management.
Programme & Impact Oversight – programme quality, beneficiary outcomes, enterprise development and impact.
Governance, Ethics & Safeguarding – institutional governance, integrity, conflict of interest, safeguarding and compliance.

For major ESO programmes, OPOLO establishes a Programme Steering Committee to provide programme-specific oversight, review performance against agreed milestones and budgets, monitor risks and ensure timely resolution of implementation issues.

Leadership and Management Structure

Day-to-day leadership is provided by Executive Management, which is accountable to the Board for translating strategy into operational plans and measurable results.

The management structure provides clear leadership across the following functions:

Programmes & Impact – responsible for entrepreneurship development, digital skills, incubation, acceleration, enterprise support and programme delivery.

Hub Operations & Service Delivery – responsible for the effective operation of OPOLO's innovation hubs, programme logistics, technology infrastructure and beneficiary support.

Finance, Risk & Compliance – responsible for budgeting, programme accounting, procurement, financial reporting, internal controls and compliance.

Partnerships & Business Development – responsible for government, corporate, development-sector, academic and ecosystem partnerships.

Talent, Investment & Market Access – responsible for employment pathways, internships, talent placement, investment readiness, investor engagement and market linkages.

Monitoring, Evaluation, Research & Learning (MERL) – responsible for performance measurement, beneficiary tracking, programme reporting, learning and impact assessment.

programmeDeliveryTrackRecord:
Past Cohorts, Programmes Delivered and Outcomes

nHub Nigeria has, since its establishment in 2015, built a strong track record of delivering structured entrepreneurship, incubation, acceleration, digital skills and enterprise-development programmes for young people, startups and MSMEs. Our experience combines cohort-based training with practical mentorship, business development support, technology enablement, market linkage and investment readiness.

One of our major entrepreneurship interventions was the Next Economy Programme (2016–2020), through which nHub supported young Nigerians with entrepreneurship, employability, business development and mentoring. The programme trained more than 1,000 young people according to nHub programme records, while its entrepreneurship component supported participants to develop and validate business ideas. nHub also facilitated crowdfunding capacity-building, with participating entrepreneurs reportedly mobilising more than ₦20 million in equity-free funding. The programme established an important foundation for nHub’s subsequent incubation and acceleration model.

nHub subsequently participated in Facebook’s 8-week incubation programme in 2019, working with selected Nigerian hubs to support startups through practical training, mentorship, prototype development and business-model refinement. This strengthened our capacity to manage structured startup cohorts and provide founders with hands-on technical and entrepreneurial support.

Through iHatch Cohort 4, implemented under the Office for Innovation and Digital Development (ONDI), nHub has continued to provide structured incubation support to emerging entrepreneurs. The programme combines founder development, mentorship, business-model refinement, validation and ecosystem connections, reinforcing nHub’s role as a startup-support organisation.

nHub has also delivered extensive development-partner-supported entrepreneurship and MSME programmes. Under GIZ/SEDIN, nHub has implemented entrepreneurship and innovation activities using structured cohort models, including the ICSS (Inspire, Create, Start and Scale) methodology. Participants receive practical entrepreneurship training, coaching, business-development support and linkages to relevant ecosystem actors. nHub has also developed and delivered digital-business capacity building for MSMEs, covering digital productivity, digital marketing, business tools, cybersecurity and technology adoption.

In 2026, nHub is implementing the iDICE Startup Bridge/Founders Lab ecosystem, supporting selected founders through onboarding, founder development, mentoring, business-model development, ecosystem networking and market/investment-readiness activities. Founders assigned to nHub operate across sectors including agriculture technology, AI/IoT, education technology, data analytics and other technology-enabled businesses.

Across these programmes, nHub’s approach has evolved from skills training to a more complete venture-development pipeline: selection and onboarding → entrepreneurship training → validation → mentorship/coaching → product/business development → market linkage → investment readiness.

The outcomes of this experience include trained entrepreneurs, strengthened startup capabilities, prototypes and business-model development, access to mentors and ecosystem partners, improved digital adoption among MSMEs, and stronger linkages between founders and markets, investors and support institutions. This cumulative experience positions nHub to deliver an effective, structured and measurable ESO programme under iDICE.

2. Job-readiness development: In addition to technical and entrepreneurial training, beneficiaries will receive practical support in CV development, portfolio building, LinkedIn and professional profiles, communication, teamwork, interview preparation, workplace behaviour and digital professionalism.

3. Industry matching: nHub will maintain an employer and industry opportunity pipeline covering technology companies, MSMEs, startups, professional service firms, development organisations and other relevant institutions. Beneficiaries will be matched to opportunities based on their skills and employer requirements.

4. Practical experience: Where feasible, nHub will facilitate internships, apprenticeships, project-based assignments, volunteering, freelance opportunities, workplace exposure and startup placements. Participants will be encouraged to demonstrate their capabilities through real projects and portfolios.

Follow-up will be conducted after placement to document outcomes, identify retention challenges and provide additional support where appropriate.

governanceStructure:
Labspace operates under a structured governance architecture designed to comply with the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA 2020) and address the operational peculiarities of running an innovation hub and ecosystem support organization (ESO) in Nigeria. The governance framework maintains a clear operational boundary between ownership, strategic oversight, and daily execution, ensuring that management operates strictly within delegated authority while key stakeholders retain necessary controls.

The governance structure comprises four primary tiers: the Shareholders, who hold primary ownership rights and decide fundamental corporate transformations; the Board of Directors, which exercises strategic oversight, risk management, and fiduciary responsibilities; Executive Management, spearheaded by the CEO/Managing Director to drive daily execution; and specialized bodies such as Board Committees, an optional non-fiduciary Advisory Board for technical domains like AI and clean energy, and ecosystem entities.

The Board of Directors functions as a cohesive fiduciary unit tasked with setting long-term strategy, ensuring regulatory compliance (including the Nigeria Startup Act 2022, tax regulations, and data protection laws), and monitoring financial sustainability. To maintain objective oversight, the framework incorporates Non-Executive Directors (NEDs) and Independent Non-Executive Directors (INEDs) appointed through a formal nomination process, subject to fixed three-year terms capped at a maximum of six to nine years, alongside mandatory retirement by rotation.

Rigorous controls govern financial management, capital raising, and risk mitigation. Executive management must adhere to a Board-approved Delegation of Authority Matrix, maintain strict segregation of financial duties, enforce dual-authorization thresholds, and comply with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering (SCUML) guidelines due to handling international donor grants and multi-currency transactions. Furthermore, strict policies govern conflict of interest, related-party transactions, and the protection of intellectual property.

To protect foundational interests, the framework establishes a Reserved Matters Matrix. While standard corporate transformations require general shareholder approval, the framework grants specific veto and control protections to the Principal Founder (while holding at least 51% of ordinary shares) over anti-dilution, board and executive control, asset and IP protection, and material financial commitments. Unresolved deadlocks are subjected to executive negotiation, mediation, and binding arbitration in Lagos, ensuring stability and business continuity for the organisation.

As a women-led innovation hub in Niger State, we treat inclusion as an operational standard rather than a compliance checkbox. Hitting the required targets 40% female representation and 5% NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) youth demands deliberate, boots-on-the-ground outreach built into every stage of the project lifecycle.

1. Targeted Mobilization & Outreach
Open calls and social media ads rarely reach underserved groups. Prior to launching recruitment, we map women-focused trade associations, youth groups, vocational centers, community radio networks, and local WhatsApp channels across the state. Leveraging our established ties with tertiary institutions, state agencies, and regional hub networks through our various existing programs,  we directly source promising candidates from our existing communities and outside conventional tech corridors.

2. Female Participation Strategy (40% Target)
To secure and maintain 40% female participation, we will tap into our already existing network of female-led networks, we engage women-led organizations as direct recruitment partners from day one. Intake data is monitored daily during the application window. If female submissions fall below our 40% benchmark at any stage of the funnel, we immediately trigger targeted community referrals and partner outreach rather than waiting until shortlisting begins.

3. NEET Youth Engagement (5% Target)
NEET youth are identified using specific baseline indicators embedded directly in our application forms. Because digital access and application literacy often pose major barriers for out-of-school or unemployed youth, we deploy assisted application support—offering both in-person assistance at the hub and guided help through local facilitators to ensure a seamless entry point.

4. Objective, Barrier-Free Selection
Selection criteria prioritize raw problem-solving ability, commitment, and practical idea viability over polished presentation skills or exposure to technical jargon. Our evaluation teams use standardized rubrics to keep scoring fair and transparent, supported by real-time demographic dashboards that track gender, geographic balance, and NEET status throughout the screening phase.

5. Retention & Practical Accessibility
Selecting participants is only the first step; keeping them engaged requires removing day-to-day friction. We accommodate different learning realities through flexible hybrid models, offline-accessible material, and scheduled check-ins to spot attendance issues early. Where participants face internet, transport, or logistical hurdles, we provide practical support to prevent dropouts.

6. Measurement, Tracking & Accountability
Inclusion metrics are tracked across every project milestone—from intake and shortlisting to graduation and post-program tracking. Regular progress reviews allow us to flag drop-off risks instantly and adjust our support strategy. This data-driven approach ensures every selected participant from an underrepresented group receives the support required to successfully complete the program and launch a viable venture.

Our relationship with AKUM has evolved beyond programme participation into institutional and ecosystem collaboration. Labspace has received and engaged with a formal proposal from the University’s Green Tech Hub to explore partnership and collaboration, positioning Labspace as a relevant ecosystem player in supporting startups, innovation and entrepreneurship. This aligns strongly with AKUM’s existing institutional architecture, which includes a Green tech and Innovation Hub, Entrepreneurship Centre and Directorate of Research, Innovation and Partnerships.

Labspace has also worked with AKUM in hosting Founders Friday Minna, a founder-centric ecosystem platform designed to connect entrepreneurs, innovators, students, investors and other ecosystem stakeholders. The relationship further deepened during the iDICE institutional inspection/evaluation process, where Labspace and AKUM jointly received and engaged the visiting iDICE evaluation team. Public records confirm AKUM's participation in the iDICE evaluation process and its selection alongside FUTMinna as one of Niger State's two iDICE host institutions.

In addition, through Tespire, a Labspace/JD Lab portfolio company and EdTech venture, the AKUM relationship extends into technology adoption and institutional digital transformation. Tespire provides education-management technology serving schools and higher institutions, creating an additional pathway for collaboration between the innovation ecosystem and the university.

- Federal University of Technology, Minna (FUTMinna):
Labspace has an established relationship with FUTMinna through direct engagement with the University's Technology Transfer Office (TTO) around innovation and technology commercialisation. Through the National Hybrid SIWES (NHS) programme, Labspace has trained and engaged FUTMinna students through structured digital-skills and employability-focused learning. The relationship has subsequently extended into the iDICE Startup Bridge Founders Lab, where Labspace continues to engage and support emerging founders and students within the university ecosystem.

These relationships give Labspace existing institutional access, stakeholder trust and practical experience that can be leveraged for beneficiary mobilisation, innovation scouting, entrepreneurship development, incubation, mentorship, technology commercialisation and sustained delivery of the proposed iDICE Centre of Excellence intervention.
institutionalCoordinationPlan:
Labspace will implement the intervention through existing institutional structures rather than creating parallel systems. Our approach will be to establish clear coordination pathways with the relevant units of each host institution, leveraging their existing student, entrepreneurship, career and innovation networks.

At Abdulkadir Kure University (AKUM), Labspace will work closely with the Greentech and Innovation & Entrepreneurship Centre, and Directorate of Research, Innovation and Partnerships to support entrepreneurship development, innovation scouting, startup identification, mentorship and technology commercialisation. These structures already have mandates aligned with the objectives of the intervention, including supporting entrepreneurial skills and innovative business ideas among students and staff. Our existing relationship with AKUM, including engagement around its Green Tech Hub, Founders Friday Minna and the iDICE institutional engagement process, will provide a strong foundation for coordination.

At FUTMinna, Labspace will coordinate with the Entrepreneurship Centre (FUTEC), Career Development Centre (CDC), Student Support Unit and relevant innovation/technology-transfer structures. FUTEC already provides entrepreneurship and skills-development programmes, while the CDC provides career counselling, professional development, internship and employment support. The Student Support Unit also has responsibilities covering career support, training and entrepreneurship skills.
Our existing relationship with FUTMinna's Technology Transfer Office, alongside our delivery of the National Hybrid SIWES programme and current iDICE engagement, provides an established pathway for student mobilisation and institutional coordination.
Across both institutions, Labspace will use these structures to support student recruitment, beneficiary identification, referrals, programme scheduling, mentorship, career and entrepreneurship support, alumni engagement and post-programme tracking. We will also activate student associations, alumni networks and relevant academic departments as referral and mobilisation channels.
This model ensures institutional ownership, reduces duplication, strengthens sustainability and enables the Centres of Excellence to become embedded within existing university systems rather than functioning as stand-alone programmes.
staffFacultyEngagementPlan:
Labspace will engage institutional staff and faculty as active partners in the delivery, sustainability and institutionalisation of the Centres of Excellence. Rather than treating faculty only as beneficiaries or administrative contacts, we will involve relevant staff as programme champions, mentors, referral partners and technical contributors.
At the commencement of the intervention, Labspace will conduct stakeholder mapping with each host institution to identify relevant faculty members and staff across entrepreneurship, innovation, technology transfer, career development, student affairs, academic departments and research/commercialisation units. Clear focal persons will be agreed with each institution to facilitate communication, scheduling, referrals and institutional decision-making.
Faculty and staff will be engaged through orientation sessions, entrepreneurship and innovation workshops, mentorship activities, founder clinics, expert sessions and innovation challenges. Faculty members with relevant industry, research or entrepreneurial expertise will be invited to serve as mentors, subject-matter experts and evaluators for student ventures. This will create opportunities for students to receive both academic and practical business guidance.
Labspace will also encourage faculty participation in innovation scouting and venture identification, enabling lecturers to refer promising student ideas, research outputs and emerging ventures into the Centre of Excellence pipeline. Relevant staff will support the identification of students who may otherwise remain outside conventional entrepreneurship programmes, including female students and underserved groups.
For AKUM, engagement will build on our existing relationship with the Greentech and Innovation Hub, Entrepreneurship Centre and Directorate of Research, Innovation and Partnerships. For FUTMinna, we will leverage our existing engagement with the Technology Transfer Office and relevant entrepreneurship, career and student-support structures.
To strengthen institutional ownership, Labspace will establish periodic faculty/staff engagement and review sessions to assess participation, student progress, emerging ventures, challenges and opportunities for improvement. We will document institutional learning and gradually strengthen the capacity of designated staff to independently coordinate entrepreneurship activities, mentorship and venture-support processes.
This approach will create a sustainable bridge between academic knowledge and entrepreneurship, while positioning faculty and institutional staff as long-term enablers of student innovation and venture development.

sustainabilityPlan:
Labspace will pursue a sustainability model that combines institutional ownership, earned revenue, strategic partnerships and ecosystem-driven opportunities to ensure that the Centres of Excellence remain active and valuable beyond the iDICE funding period.

1. Institutional ownership and integration:
From inception, Labspace will work with AKUM and FUTMinna to embed entrepreneurship, innovation and venture-support activities within existing institutional structures, including the Entrepreneurship Centres, Greentech and Innovation Hub, Technology Transfer Office and Career Services. Staff and faculty will progressively be equipped to support programme delivery, mentorship and venture development, reducing long-term dependence on external programme managers.

2. Paid entrepreneurship and skills programmes:
Labspace will develop paid versions of selected capacity-building offerings for students, graduates, staff, MSMEs and external participants. These may include entrepreneurship bootcamps, digital skills, AI for business, financial literacy, innovation management, pitch development and investment-readiness programmes. Institutional and corporate sponsorships will also be pursued to subsidise participation for students who cannot afford paid programmes.

3. Incubation and venture-support services:
The Centres will develop a pipeline of promising ventures that can access structured incubation, business validation, advisory, pitch preparation, market-access and investment-readiness support. Selected advanced services can operate on a fee-for-service basis, while maintaining free or subsidised entry-level support for student innovators.

4. Corporate and ecosystem partnerships:
Labspace will leverage its existing relationships across the innovation, development and private sectors to attract corporate sponsorships, sponsored innovation challenges, scholarships, entrepreneurship programmes and industry-led skills initiatives. Partners will be offered opportunities to engage with emerging talent, startups and university innovation pipelines.

5. Events, innovation challenges and ecosystem activities:
Founder events, Demo Days, innovation showcases, competitions and industry networking activities will provide additional opportunities for sponsorship, partnerships and paid participation while continuously generating visibility and new opportunities for beneficiaries.

6. Alumni and venture ecosystem:
Beneficiaries will be maintained within an alumni network, creating a continuous pipeline of mentors, founders, employers, investors and ecosystem partners. Successful ventures can subsequently become mentors, partners, service providers or sponsors, creating a reinforcing ecosystem.
Our sustainability objective is therefore to transition from programme-funded delivery to an institutionally embedded, partnership-driven and increasingly revenue-generating model, while retaining inclusive access for students and underserved innovators.

governanceStructure:
Governance Structure

The proposed governance structure for the iDICE Centre will ensure clear accountability, effective programme delivery, strong financial controls, industry relevance and institutional sustainability. It will operate through four interconnected levels: Programme Oversight, Steering Committee, Programme Management, and Industry & Ecosystem Advisory support.

1. Programme Oversight

The iDICE Programme Coordination Unit (PCU) and Aggregator Consortium will provide programme-level oversight, quality assurance and monitoring in accordance with the iDICE implementation framework. The ESO will maintain regular reporting and coordination with the Aggregator throughout implementation.

2. Programme Steering Committee

A Programme Steering Committee will provide strategic governance and ensure alignment between the ESO, host institution and iDICE objectives. Membership will include representatives of the ESO, host institution, Programme Director and relevant industry/ecosystem stakeholders. The Committee will review implementation plans, programme performance, financial utilisation, risks, compliance and sustainability. It will meet quarterly or as required.

3. Programme Management

Day-to-day implementation will be led by a dedicated Programme Director/Centre Director, who will serve as the principal accountable officer and primary interface with the Aggregator and host institution.

Three functional pillars will report to the Programme Director:

Programme Delivery: Training and Curriculum; Incubation and Acceleration; Mentorship and Business Advisory; Industry Partnerships and Job Placement; and Ecosystem Development.
Operations & Finance: Finance and Grants Management; Procurement; Administration; Human Resources; logistics; and Centre operations.
Monitoring, Evaluation, Risk & Compliance: Monitoring and Evaluation; data and reporting; safeguarding; Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI); grievance management; data protection; and programme compliance.

Strong financial governance will be maintained through a dedicated project account/sub-ledger, segregation of financial responsibilities, documented procurement procedures, approval limits, regular reconciliation and quarterly financial reporting.

4. Industry & Ecosystem Advisory Council

An Industry & Ecosystem Advisory Council comprising private-sector employers, technology and creative-industry leaders, investors, professional bodies and ecosystem partners will provide market intelligence and strengthen pathways to mentorship, internships, employment, investment and commercial opportunities.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity:
Strategy to Achieve 40% Female and 5% NEET Youth Participation

Black Accelerate will adopt a targeted, inclusive recruitment and retention strategy to ensure that at least 40% of programme beneficiaries are female and a minimum of 5% are NEET youth (Not in Education, Employment or Training). Inclusion targets will be embedded into beneficiary mobilisation, selection, programme delivery and performance monitoring from inception.

For female participation, Black Accelerate will undertake targeted outreach through universities, women-focused technology and entrepreneurship communities, professional associations, community organisations and female-led businesses. Recruitment campaigns will feature female role models and mentors and deliberately communicate opportunities in technology, entrepreneurship and the creative economy to women. A minimum 40% female participation threshold will be incorporated into cohort selection, with applications monitored throughout the recruitment period to enable corrective mobilisation where participation is below target.

For NEET youth, recruitment will extend beyond conventional university and online channels. Black Accelerate will work with community-based organisations, local government structures, youth associations, vocational centres, faith-based/community networks and grassroots organisations to identify young people who are currently outside education, employment and formal training. At least 5% of available programme places will be deliberately reserved for eligible NEET participants.

Participation barriers will also be addressed through flexible programme schedules, blended learning where appropriate, accessible training locations, mentoring and targeted participant support. Where programme resources permit, interventions such as transportation support, internet/data access and access to devices will be considered for beneficiaries whose circumstances could otherwise prevent sustained participation.

Black Accelerate will establish a Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) monitoring framework to track applications, selection, enrolment, attendance, completion and outcomes by gender and beneficiary category. A designated GESI focal person will review performance regularly and initiate targeted recruitment or retention interventions where participation begins to fall below the required thresholds.

Beyond enrolment, success will be measured by completion and economic outcomes. Female and NEET beneficiaries will receive equal access to mentorship, internships, incubation, employment opportunities, enterprise support and investor/market linkages.

Through targeted recruitment, reserved participation thresholds, removal of access barriers and continuous monitoring, Black Accelerate will ensure that the 40% female and 5% NEET targets translate into meaningful participation, programme completion and sustainable economic opportunities, rather than simply meeting enrolment quotas.

beneficiaryReferralPlan:

Faculty members and designated Faculty Champions will refer promising innovators, researchers and students, while Career Services and Student Affairs will support identification of beneficiaries requiring employability, digital-skills and entrepreneurship interventions. Beyond the host institution, Black Accelerate will leverage its network of innovation hubs, industry partners, community organisations, professional associations and entrepreneurship networks to reach eligible beneficiaries, particularly underserved groups and NEET youth who may not be accessible through conventional university channels.

All referred candidates will be directed to a centralised application and registration process to ensure fairness and consistency. Applicants will be assessed against clearly defined eligibility and selection criteria, including programme fit, motivation, innovation or enterprise potential and readiness to participate. A beneficiary database will track each participant from referral and application through selection, onboarding, programme participation, completion and post-programme outcomes. This will enable Black Accelerate and the host institution to monitor recruitment sources, participation, retention and impact.

monitoringReportingSystems:

Data quality will be protected through defined collection protocols, verification checks, periodic audits and clear accountability for data entry and approval. sustainabilityPlan:

From inception, Black Accelerate will work with the host institution to integrate the Centre into existing entrepreneurship, innovation, career-development and research-commercialisation structures, while progressively transferring programme knowledge, systems and operational capabilities to designated institutional staff.

Revenue diversification will be pursued through multiple channels. The Centre will also develop corporate sponsorship and partnership arrangements with technology companies, financial institutions, telecommunications companies and other private-sector organisations. Where appropriate, sustainable commercial arrangements may also be developed around startups and innovations emerging from the Centre, subject to agreed programme and institutional policies.

Black Accelerate will actively pursue grants and programme funding from government agencies, development finance institutions, foundations and international development organisations to finance specialised programmes and expand the Centre's reach.

The Centre will also strengthen relationships with angel investors, venture capital firms, financial institutions and corporate innovation teams, creating investment and commercialisation pathways for promising ventures while increasing the Centre's attractiveness as an innovation and entrepreneurship platform.

employmentPathway:
Black Accelerate will implement a structured employment pathway that connects beneficiaries directly from skills development to practical industry experience and ultimately to paid employment, freelancing or enterprise opportunities.

The pathway will begin with beneficiary profiling and skills assessment during onboarding to establish each participant’s competencies, career interests and employment readiness. Based on this assessment, beneficiaries will be assigned to appropriate technical and career-development tracks aligned with identified industry demand.

Training will combine technical skills with workplace-readiness competencies, including communication, teamwork, problem-solving, project management, CV development, interview preparation, portfolio development and professional conduct. Participants will also work on practical projects and industry-led briefs, enabling them to demonstrate applied capabilities rather than relying solely on training certificates.

Black Accelerate will engage its network of corporate organisations, technology companies, startups, SMEs and ecosystem partners to provide internships, apprenticeships, project-based assignments and entry-level employment opportunities. Employer partners will be engaged early in programme delivery to validate skills requirements, provide mentors and identify potential candidates for recruitment.

A dedicated Industry Partnerships and Placement function will maintain an employer opportunity pipeline and match qualified beneficiaries with available internships and jobs. Career fairs, employer sessions, recruitment days and curated interviews will provide direct interaction between beneficiaries and prospective employers.

The employment pathway will follow a clearly defined progression:

Recruitment & Assessment → Skills Development → Practical/Industry Projects → Career Readiness → Internship/Apprenticeship → Employer Matching → Interviews → Employment/Contract Placement → Post-Placement Tracking

For beneficiaries pursuing independent careers, the programme will provide pathways into freelancing, entrepreneurship and startup development, including business advisory, incubation, market access and connections to potential clients and investors.

Employment outcomes will be tracked beyond programme completion, including internships secured, job placements, freelance contracts, businesses established and income-generating opportunities. Employer feedback will also be used to improve subsequent training cohorts.

Training and capacity development: Delivery of fee-based entrepreneurship, digital skills, employability, financial literacy, business management and other professional development programmes for institutions, organisations and private-sector clients.

employmentPathway:
Bugbafu Consult Limited will implement a structured training-to-employment pathway designed to ensure that iDICE beneficiaries move beyond acquiring skills to accessing concrete employment, internship, apprenticeship or self-employment opportunities.

The pathway will begin with beneficiary profiling and career/enterprise assessment to understand each participant’s existing skills, interests, experience and employment aspirations. Participants will then receive relevant digital, entrepreneurship and employability training, with emphasis on practical competencies that respond to identified opportunities in the labour market.

Following training, beneficiaries will be supported through practical projects, business challenges, mentoring, workplace-readiness sessions and portfolio development. Participants pursuing employment will be assisted to develop CVs, professional profiles, portfolios and interview skills, while those pursuing entrepreneurship will receive business-model development, enterprise diagnostics, market validation and business-support services.

Bugbafu will then activate its institutional, private-sector and ecosystem networks to facilitate referrals to employers, internships, apprenticeships, freelance opportunities, industry mentors, technology enterprises, MSMEs and other relevant organisations. Alumni and professionals within partner institutions and innovation hubs will also be engaged to provide industry exposure, mentoring and employment leads.

For participants who demonstrate viable entrepreneurial potential, the pathway will provide an alternative route into self-employment and enterprise growth through business incubation, mentoring, access-to-finance referrals, market linkages and digital-business support. This approach builds on Bugbafu Consult’s previous experience in youth employability and entrepreneurship programmes, including the Federal Government Graduate Internship Scheme, U-WIN Connect and youth empowerment initiatives, as well as its broader experience in enterprise development and MSME support.

The ultimate objective is to create a clear and measurable pathway from learning to earning—ensuring that iDICE beneficiaries acquire relevant skills, demonstrate practical competence, connect with employers or markets, and transition into sustainable employment or viable entrepreneurship.

governanceStructure:
Corestream Networks and Robotics Limited (RC 1512578) operates a functional reporting structure built around a small executive management team, five operational department heads, and clearly defined lines of accountability from strategy down to service delivery.

At the apex of the structure sits the Chief Executive Officer, Ibrahim Akorede Jimoh, who holds overall responsibility for corporate strategy, partnerships, investor relations, and product innovation. The CEO is supported by two C-suite executives and a Director of Learning, together forming the core executive management team that sets organisational direction and approves major decisions.

The Chief Technology Officer, Walshak Timothy, leads all engineering, artificial intelligence, infrastructure, and architecture functions. Reporting into this office are five technical teams: Software Engineering, Mobile Development, AI & Research, DevOps & Infrastructure, and Quality Assurance. This structure allows Corestream to develop and maintain its core products — including CoreHealth and Wecare247 — while continuing applied research and platform-level infrastructure work in parallel.

The Chief Operating Officer, Shamsudeen Abdulrazak, oversees Operations, spanning Finance, Human Resources, Procurement, Administration, and Compliance. This office ensures the organisation's internal controls, statutory compliance, and administrative systems are sound enough to support both commercial contracts and government-facing engagements.

The Director of Learning, Sudais Abubakar, heads the Learning function, which delivers the company's training and capacity-building programmes — including 4E Africa and Coreskool — through a team of Training Coordinators and Facilitators. This division is central to Corestream's ability to execute large-scale, multi-state skills and education programmes.

Two further functional areas complete the operational structure: a Business Development Lead, responsible for Sales, Partnerships, and Marketing, who drives client acquisition and strategic alliances; and a Digital Health Division, covering CoreHealth, Wecare247, Implementations, and Customer Success, which manages hospital deployments and ongoing client support.

Governance follows a five-step accountability loop. First, Executive Management sets strategic direction. Second, department heads (the CTO, COO, Director of Learning, Business Development Lead, and Digital Health lead) translate that direction into operational plans for their respective functions. Third, team leads within each department supervise day-to-day project execution. Fourth, technical and support staff carry out the actual delivery of products and services. Fifth, and critically, performance data and outcomes flow back up through the same channels to Executive Management, which reviews results and adjusts strategy accordingly — closing the loop rather than leaving reporting as a one-way process.

This structure currently supports a workforce of 38 — 4 in executive leadership, 16 in Technology, 6 in Digital Health, 7 in Learning, and 5 in Operations & Administration — of whom 31 are full-time employees and 7 are engaged on a project basis, allowing the organisation to flex capacity for time-bound programmes without disrupting its core team.

Taken together, this governance model gives Corestream a structure that is deliberately compact at the top for fast decision-making, while functionally organised beneath it to run software development, digital health, AI, EdTech, government digital transformation, technical skills development, and innovation programmes simultaneously — with clear reporting lines and a built-in feedback mechanism for continuous improvement.

inclusionAccessibilityCapacity:
Inclusion & Accessibility Capacity

Corestream's inclusion strategy is built on a track record, not just a target: our current IDEAS Project TVET cohort already stands at 63% female participation, well above the 40% benchmark, demonstrating that our recruitment and delivery model organically attracts and retains women. We will replicate and formalise this approach across all programme sites to sustain the 40% female target while building deliberate, additional pathways to reach 5% NEET (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) youth.

Reaching the 40% Female Target

Community-based recruitment: Partner with women's associations, faith-based groups, and local female role models (as already demonstrated in the IDEAS cohort) to drive trusted, peer-led outreach rather than generic advertising.
Female facilitators and mentors: Deploy women instructors and industry mentors visibly across cohorts so prospective female learners see relatable role models in technical and creative roles.
Safe, flexible learning environments: Offer training slots and formats (morning/afternoon options, hybrid delivery) that accommodate caregiving responsibilities, and ensure venues are safe and culturally appropriate, particularly in northern Nigeria.
Targeted messaging: Design outreach materials that explicitly welcome women into technology, robotics, and digital health tracks — areas where female enrolment is traditionally lower — rather than only Creative Media, where uptake is already strong.

Reaching the 5% NEET Youth Target

Direct partnership with NEET-serving structures: Work with state employment agencies, vocational centres, youth corps offices (NYSC), and community/religious leaders to identify and refer NEET youth who are outside conventional school or job networks.
Reduced-barrier entry: Waive formal prerequisite qualifications for NEET applicants, replacing them with an aptitude-based screening and orientation bootcamp to bring participants up to cohort-ready level.
Stipends and transport support: Provide modest participation incentives (transport allowance, data/airtime support) to offset the opportunity cost that often prevents NEET youth from completing training.
Wraparound support: Pair NEET participants with dedicated mentors and our M&E team for closer attendance tracking, given this group's higher risk of drop-off, and connect them early to the 4E Africa Employment pillar (internships, apprenticeships, startup incubation) so the training visibly leads somewhere.

Monitoring & Accountability

Disaggregate all enrolment, attendance, and outcome data by gender and NEET status from intake through graduation, reviewed monthly by the M&E Officer.
Set cohort-level minimums (not just programme-wide averages) so no single track or location falls below target, and course-correct recruitment mid-cycle where needed.
Report inclusion metrics alongside standard delivery metrics in every stakeholder and partner report, ensuring transparency on both female and NEET participation.

This combination of proven community trust (already yielding 63% female participation), deliberate NEET outreach infrastructure, and disaggregated monitoring positions Corestream not merely to meet but to sustainably exceed the 40% female and 5% NEET targets across the programme's life.

programmeDeliveryTrackRecord:
Aikperokha Innovation Hub Ltd has built practical experience in delivering entrepreneurship, technology, digital skills, incubation, mentorship and enterprise development programmes for young people, students, entrepreneurs and early-stage startups in Kogi State and the wider North Central ecosystem.

Since commencing operations, the Hub has supported 15+ startups and entrepreneurs through structured business development guidance, mentorship, digital skills development, product development, customer validation and growth support. Our activities have included capacity-building sessions, boot camps, entrepreneurship workshops, founder advisory sessions, mentorship engagements and practical learning activities designed to help participants develop market-relevant skills and build sustainable ventures.

Aikperokha has also gained direct programme delivery experience through its participation in the iDICE Startup Bridge – Founders Lab, where the Hub supported assigned founders through structured programme activities, including one-on-one advisory sessions, business model development, customer discovery, MVP development, market validation, pitch preparation, financial planning and investment readiness. The experience strengthened our capacity to work with founders at different stages of development, monitor progress and provide targeted support based on individual venture needs.

During the Founders Lab engagement, the Hub facilitated and monitored founder participation, provided advisory support and encouraged practical validation of business ideas. Founders received guidance in areas such as identifying customer problems, refining value propositions, developing MVPs, preparing for pilots, improving business models and preparing for funding and investment opportunities.

Beyond startup support, Aikperokha has organised and facilitated entrepreneurship and digital skills activities for young people, including engagements with secondary school and university students. These activities have focused on entrepreneurship awareness, digital skills, innovation, career development and exposure to technology-enabled opportunities.

The Hub also maintains connections across the wider ecosystem, including engagements and collaborations involving organisations such as iHATCH Nigeria and WorldQuant University, as well as entrepreneurs, technology professionals, mentors, educators and other ecosystem stakeholders. These relationships enhance our ability to connect beneficiaries with relevant expertise, learning opportunities and industry exposure.

Our programme delivery model combines participant mobilisation, structured learning, practical workshops, mentorship, one-on-one support, founder check-ins, ecosystem engagement, attendance monitoring, progress tracking and outcome documentation. We use participant feedback and progress information to identify challenges early and adapt support where necessary.

Aikperokha has developed the operational capacity to coordinate physical and virtual sessions, manage participant communication, engage mentors and facilitators, maintain programme records, monitor participation and prepare stakeholder reports.

With a physical presence in Lokoja, Kogi State, an understanding of the local entrepreneurial ecosystem and experience supporting early-stage ventures, Aikperokha is positioned to deliver an inclusive, practical and outcome-focused programme that connects beneficiaries to skills, mentorship, industry, markets and investment opportunities.

sustainabilityPlan:

The objective is to build a financially sustainable innovation hub capable of continuing enterprise and digital skills support beyond the programme funding period.

1. Membership and Coworking Services:
The Hub will generate recurring revenue through affordable community and coworking memberships, providing access to workspace, internet, meeting facilities, networking and selected business support services. Flexible membership packages will serve students, freelancers, startups, SMEs and professionals.

2. Paid Training and Professional Development:
Aikperokha will offer affordable paid training, boot camps and masterclasses in areas such as digital skills, data science, software development, cloud technologies, product management, entrepreneurship and business development. Advanced programmes and specialised corporate training will provide additional revenue.

3. Incubation and Business Support Services:
The Hub will provide fee-based services including business plan development, product advisory, market research, customer validation, pitch preparation, digital product support and business growth consulting. Selected startups may also access structured incubation and acceleration packages.

4. Corporate Partnerships and Sponsorships:
Aikperokha will develop partnerships with companies, financial institutions, technology organisations, development organisations and other private-sector stakeholders to sponsor training cohorts, innovation challenges, entrepreneurship events and youth development initiatives.

5. Grants and Programme Funding:
The Hub will continue to pursue competitive grants and programme funding from government agencies, development partners, foundations and ecosystem programmes. Grants will complement rather than replace earned revenue and will be targeted toward activities with measurable social and economic impact.

6. Industry and Ecosystem Partnerships:
Relationships with organisations such as iHATCH Nigeria, WorldQuant University and other ecosystem stakeholders will be strengthened to create opportunities for technical training, mentorship, referrals, industry engagement and joint programmes.

7. Digital and Knowledge Products:
The Hub will progressively develop digital learning resources, workshops, templates and other knowledge products that can generate additional income while expanding access beyond the physical hub.

Aikperokha will monitor revenue by stream, manage operating costs and reinvest a portion of earnings into infrastructure, programme delivery and community support. This diversified model will reduce dependence on a single funding source and strengthen the Hub's ability to sustain its operations and continue supporting entrepreneurs and young people in North Central Nigeria.
employmentPathway:
Aikperokha Innovation Hub Ltd will create a practical pathway that connects programme beneficiaries from skills development to employability, internships, industry exposure, entrepreneurship and employment opportunities. The approach will combine technical training, career preparation, employer engagement and post-programme referrals.

1. Skills and Career Assessment:
At onboarding, beneficiaries will be profiled based on their existing skills, interests, career goals and areas requiring development. This will enable the Hub to align participants with relevant learning tracks and potential industry opportunities.

2. Industry-Relevant Skills Development:
Participants will receive practical training in areas such as digital technology, data, software development, cloud technologies, product development, creative skills, entrepreneurship and business development. Training will emphasise practical projects and portfolio development so participants can demonstrate their capabilities to prospective employers.

3. Career Readiness:
The Hub will provide support with CV development, LinkedIn profiles, portfolios, interview preparation, communication skills, professional conduct and job-search strategies. Participants will also be guided on freelance, remote-work and entrepreneurial opportunities where appropriate.

4. Industry Engagement:
Aikperokha will leverage its ecosystem relationships with technology professionals, entrepreneurs, businesses, iHATCH Nigeria, WorldQuant University and other relevant stakeholders to facilitate industry talks, mentorship, networking, workplace exposure and referrals.

5. Internship and Apprenticeship Pathways:
Where opportunities are available, qualified participants will be referred to companies, startups, SMEs and ecosystem organisations for internships, apprenticeships, project placements and work-based learning. Placement will be matched to participants' skills and career interests.

6. Employer and Opportunity Matching:
The Hub will maintain an opportunity pipeline covering jobs, internships, freelance engagements, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship opportunities. Participants who meet relevant requirements will be referred to suitable opportunities, while employers and partners can access a pool of trained emerging talent.

7. Entrepreneurship as an Employment Pathway:
Participants interested in entrepreneurship will receive support to validate business ideas, develop MVPs, identify customers, build business models and pursue market and funding opportunities. This creates pathways for participants to become job creators as well as job seekers.

8. Post-Programme Tracking:
Aikperokha will maintain alumni records and conduct follow-ups to track employment, internships, business launches, additional training and other outcomes. Lessons from these results will inform future industry engagement and programme delivery.

This pathway ensures that programme participation extends beyond training and provides beneficiaries with practical routes into employment, work experience, self-employment and enterprise growth.

governanceStructure:
MountMove Global is led by the CEO, supported by four permanent staff, 12 part-time or freelance specialists, and six industry mentors.

The Board comprises the CEO/Managing Director and a part-time Non-Executive Chair with finance and governance experience. Its responsibilities include approving strategy and budgets, reviewing risks, overseeing major commitments and holding executive leadership accountable.
The CEO manages daily operations. We allocate the four permanent roles across operations and delivery, technology and engineering, business growth and advisory, and training and incubation, with clear responsibilities and reporting lines.
A three-member Advisory Board would provide independent guidance on technology and AI, finance and commercial growth, and enterprise development. The members were drawn from our six industry mentors. Advisers support decision-making without statutory voting or executive authority.
We have quarterly board and advisory meetings, monthly management reviews, documented decisions, delegated spending limits and conflict-of-interest declarations. programmeDeliveryTrackRecord:

The completed Nigeria and Sheffield programme combined online sessions with community learning days and tracked participant confidence and digital skills. Outreach will explain the programme’s benefits, participation requirements and available support in plain language. Female trainers, mentors and participant stories will help prospective applicants see themselves in the programme.
We will aim to recruit 45% women and 8% NEET youth, providing a margin above the minimum targets. We will review applications weekly, extend targeted outreach where representation is low, and maintain a reserve list. Applications will be available through online forms and assisted telephone or community registration. Selection will consider motivation and potential without requiring previous technical experience.
NEET applicants will receive a supportive onboarding conversation to identify barriers and agree learning goals. We will establish eligibility through proportionate self-declaration and any evidence required by the funder. Young women who are NEET may contribute to both inclusion targets, while each participant counts once within the overall cohort.
Before delivery, we will assess participants’ access to devices, connectivity, suitable study space and accessibility support. Within the programme budget, we will prioritise data assistance, transport support for essential physical sessions and practical arrangements for participants with caring responsibilities. We will explore device access through community partners where necessary.
Delivery will combine predictable schedules, flexible catch-up opportunities and accessible learning materials. These will include recordings, captions or transcripts, readable documents, clear visual layouts and materials that work on mobile phones with limited bandwidth. Facilitators will explain unfamiliar terminology and provide relevant local examples. Any physical venues will be assessed for accessibility, and individual support needs will inform reasonable adjustments.
The Training and Incubation Lead will coordinate inclusion, supported by Operations and Delivery. Trainers and mentors will receive guidance on inclusive facilitation, respectful communication and responding to participation barriers. A named safeguarding contact, clear conduct expectations and confidential reporting routes will help create a learning environment where participants can raise concerns safely.
We will track attendance, engagement and progression through a monitoring dashboard. Early absences will trigger supportive contact, followed by an agreed recovery plan where appropriate. Monthly reviews will examine female and NEET participation, retention, completion and feedback, with corrective actions assigned to named staff.
We will collect only necessary participant information, explain its purpose and restrict access. Funder will receive aggregated results. Success will mean meeting representation targets while enabling participants to complete meaningful projects, demonstrate stronger skills and identify realistic routes towards employment, further learning or enterprise.
